utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should explain at the outset that we are late in starting because we had some technical issues that had to be resolved. Mr. Tapuskovic, you are to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, thank you. With us is Awuskha Laloe, who is an intern of ours. She is here to try and enhance our ability to communicate with the accused. I thought it necessary to advise you on her presence here, on the presence of another member of the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's very good of you, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, let us pick up where we left off a few days ago. First of all, to start with, can you tell the Judges when you joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in the second half of May or in early June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges something about the place where you were. Who were the people there who joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you something about the territory where I was. On that territory, the people who joined were mainly the local citizens and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which brigade was that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, it was called the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you mean by saying at first it was called the Ilijas Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that the Ilijas Brigade as such existed until 1994. I was a member of it. As of 1994, my area of responsibility fell under another brigade, when General Milosevic assumed command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who commanded that brigade when the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps commander was General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st Romanija brigade that I was a member of was Colonel Vlado Lizdek.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges when General Dragomir Milosevic assumed command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milosevic assumed command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in the summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until his arrival, what were you doing in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? What were you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, in 1992, and the first half of it was relatively calm, I was a private.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you well, you mentioned 1992 and you said that it was calm.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I may explain. In the territory where I was, until mid-June of that year, until the 12th of June, that territory was pretty calm. Until the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina carried out a mass murder in the village of Crmaljino [phoen], which is not far from our -- my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did happen exactly?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning, at dawn, one could hear shooting from my village. We didn't know what was happening. It lasted shortly, I'd say for a few hours. After that, we learned that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Muslim forces entered the village and committed a disgraceful act, that is, the people that were found were killed and houses set on fire. They destroyed the property there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm actually I'm raising on the point of relevancy and one might have expected, but relevancy because while I see we are outside of the indictment period and far outside of the indictment period, we actually have no idea what area this witness is talking about other than maybe somewhere in the municipality of Ilijas, and I for one, Your Honour, am not in a position to even preliminarily assess the relevancy until we have some further definition or understanding of exactly where he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you have heard the objection. What is your response to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to try to get from the witness some additional information about where Ilijas is, in whose area of responsibility it is, and I believe that the time of the beginning of the conflict is of importance in order to understand the behaviour of those people who took up arms. The general context, that is. Which is very important. I've only just begun examining the witness on that and I wanted to gain some explanation in order for the Chamber to understand where Ilijas is and whether it was within the AOR of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that by itself wouldn't make it relevant, even if it were within the area of responsibility of the corps. Please remember the golden rule that evidence of Serb suffering is not by itself necessarily relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we'll allow you to go further but you must establish very quickly the relevance of this evidence, otherwise, I'll tell to you proceed to another area of evidence that is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness spontaneously said some things I had not asked about. I did not stop him, though. I tried to move on to 1994. However, the witness volunteered the information about 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why don't you just move on? I've said that I allowed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, when you said that you were a member of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, at that time in 1994 what were you then exactly at the moment when the 1st Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was commanded by General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, too, I was a soldier, a member of the army of the Republika Srpska, when General Milosevic assumed the command of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were your tasks up until that time?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that, I was a tank driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what was it that happened in 1994 that remains etched in your memory as something of importance, before General Dragomir Milosevic assumed his position?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I failed to understand, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did something happen that year, something that had to do with heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It did have to do with the heavy weaponry. I, as an ordinary soldier remember General Milosevic because, at that time, heavy weaponry with withdrawn outside of the immediate zone of 20 kilometres. Also, during some intensive offensives, he managed to stop Muslims from advancing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said you were a tank driver. That year after the heavy weapons were withdrawn outside of the 20-kilometre zone were there any changes in your unit?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I wanted to say before you interrupted me. What I mentioned the pull-out of the heavy weapons out of the 20-kilometre zone, tanks were pulled out as well, and guns, Howitzers, mortars, and all that happened during General Milosevic's time. It was withdrawn and deployed in the wider area of the Nisici plateau. That's whey now about. However I heard of another area at Trnovo that there too a large number of pieces were pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why in those two particular areas or directions?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's clear if I say outside of the 20-kilometre zone, starting from Sarajevo, that it means that it was the area of the 1st Romanija Brigade. At Nisici, the distance is about 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any other assignments? Before that you had driven a tank. Were you given any other assignments or any other pieces of equipment?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to explain it to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes. After three additional tanks arrived, a tank platoon was formed. The platoon was commanded at first Panto Bozic and since I was the one who was the most familiar with the area, I was appointed as his deputy in that part of the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know from which locations those tanks arrived?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those tanks came from Sarajevo, for the most part. From Ilijas, Hadzic, and Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a map which will enable us to explain things further to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is DD00-4064. It is one of the maps out of a set of maps forwarded by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please indicate the Ilijas municipality, where you lived and tell us to which town it belonged?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about the Ilijas municipality, it's a part of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please indicate the boundaries.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of what you marked there, are you able to point out for the Judges how many municipalities there were in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town of Sarajevo consisted of the following municipalities. Ilijas to the north, that would be the municipality of Ilijas, bordering on Vogosca municipality; then Centar; Novi Grad including new Sarajevo; Hadzici; Ilidza; new Sarajevo; Trnovo; old town, Stari Grad; and Pale. Excuse me, please, I apologise for my markings, but basically that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the geographic characteristics of the territories of Ilidza, Stari Grad, Novi Grad, Novo Sarajevo? Could you please indicate a few points that you know are higher points in relation to their surroundings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you would just need to give me a little bit more time, because they are hard to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you go from municipality to municipality, you can just give us an approximate position.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can talk about the approximate position in the municipalities that I'm particularly familiar with, and that would be Ilijas, Vogosca, Hadzici, and Ilidza municipalities, where I had many relatives of mine. I'm going to start from Ilijas. Is it necessary to actually mark the places or just to speak about them?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These points that have to do with the municipalities of Ilidza, Vogosca, Centar, can you please tell us something about that, if you were in a position to be familiar with these places, as you said?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I left my home in 1994 and fled to the Vogosca municipality, I can then describe the characteristics for that area. The dominant elevations that were held by the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Vogosca were as follows. Zuc as one of the most dominant elevations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please indicate that with a circle?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot find it here. I know where it is in my head but I really cannot see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, then, just wait for a second. Can you at least indicate the places in Vogosca, Ilidza, and Centar if you're unable to point them out?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vogosca it was Zuc, Orlic, Hum, these were the most important and the highest elevations under the control of -- they were controlled from the town via the Rosulje Hotun settlements. The second municipality that I can mention is Hadzici. Then Ilidza. That's where the Mount Igman was, which is over 1600 metres above sea level. Then Crni Vrh, Golo Brdo, those areas also made it possible to have control over the southern part of Trnovo municipality. Also Mount Orman, which is about 1.200 metres high, and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also tell us something about the southern area, tell us what you know and then we can finish with that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality here in the southern part is Mojmilo. Actually, Mojmilo is one of the most important elevations through which it was possible to control the entire area of Grbavica as well as the Grbavica-Vrace road, and that then goes in the direction of the north-east towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that all this was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And were any of those elevations under the control of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about these dominant elevations, which I mentioned, especially elevations Zuc, Orlic, and the others that I mentioned, the other ones, these elevations were held by the Muslims by The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The -- they -- those forces held the main peak. The lines of separation were close to that, some 100 metres off, so that when we're talking about these dominant elevations what I would like to say, also when we're talking about the city of Sarajevo, is that besides the dominant elevations there were also some other locations, buildings or facilities that were built and that were under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that offered a view overlooking the elevations and the points held by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I asked if you knew about any elevation that was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska to the east and did you know --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has gone on for some time now and perhaps my fault in that I let it go, but this whole line of questioning is without any foundation whatsoever to underpin the witness' answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you mean by it's lacking in foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we still don't know where he was serving in his own municipality and now we're on the far west side or the south side of Sarajavo without any evidence of whether he's visited these areas, he's received reports about any events going on these areas, he's had any experience in mapping so he's able to talk about the heights that he is discussing with such knowledge and familiarity. I would suggest, Your Honour, there is no foundation and the line of question is inappropriate up to this point without that being established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you must get from the witness the basis of his knowledge of these matters. How did he acquire this knowledge and familiarity with these matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, you heard what His Honour Judge Robinson said and I wanted to ask you as this is very important how you happen to know all of this, that the elevations were of such characteristics and under whose control they were. Were you familiar with that as a soldier? Simply, can you please say how you knew these things?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll just be very simple. This is the territory of the town of Sarajevo and I indicated that in red marker. This is the place where I was born, the town of Ilijas. I went to school in Ilidza. I had close relatives throughout Sarajevo. I had relatives in each municipality, close relatives. When we look at the distance of the municipalities that I talked about, it's a fact that they're all very close. As a pupil and student since I attended the forestry technical school before the war and I'm very familiar with these areas, especially the part of Ilidza, yes, Ilidza and Mount Igman, which we actually -- or where we actually planted trees during our studies when we would come to specific places, elevations the professors would show us what could be seen and what was known about that particular place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And can you explain to the Judges now how you know who was at those elevations during the conflict. How did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, well, it's just like I answered earlier. It's logical. If I had relatives in the Vogosca municipality, that was holding the lines in the Vogosca municipality in Sarajevo, then it was known, if the length of the lines was 150 metres, who was up and who was down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this map please be tendered as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, before we take a position on that, I would suggest that you ask the witness to mark with letters some of the circles that he has made, because otherwise it will be impossible for us understand what the map means subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do that, Your Honour, Judge Harhoff. I meant to do that, but I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This place where you were born, can you please indicate the circle that you made with the mark the circle with the letter K. And the place where you went to school, can you mark that with a letter R?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: One of the arrows, the one indicating to the right, can you place the letter P there, and I'm going to say that in all of these directions the witness had relatives that he visited frequently and he went to this -- these areas as a -- as a pupil. So can you please indicate all of these areas with the letter T.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also tell the Judges where you worked. Where was your job located, if you can tell us that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't work before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You came from the army and when the war broke out you didn't have a job?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I wanted to tell all of that from the beginning as a complete story but I kept being interrupted all the time and that's why my testimony seems to have become quite complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you had some health problems so we have to use the time that we have left for more important things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this exhibit, this map to be exhibited in this form, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D280, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Judges how many tanks your unit had at a certain point?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was formed, my unit had five tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened when, in the summer of 1994, General Dragomir Milosevic became the commanding officer of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps? What happened in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When General Milosevic came to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as its commander, the following things happened. Since he stopped the offensives at Serb positions and established lines of defence, a truce came in late 1994 and early 1995, I think, which was absolutely respected from our side. Perhaps there was some shooting from infantry weapons on the line, but that is not important. While on the other side --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said June 1994 was the month that he came there. What happened towards the end of 1994? Did something happened in late 1994, in particular where you were?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1994, I think in November, there was an attack in the wider area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The attack was thwarted, and lines of defence were established along the entire zone of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet General Milosevic in person during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the conflict, I was wounded. I never met General Milosevic at that time. However, I did get to meet him in 1995, in February I believe, when he personally visited my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where and how did you get wounded, and when?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wounded three times. The last time was one and a half kilometres away from my house in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After that activity in November which was stopped, what followed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I returned to my unit and was appointed deputy commander of the tank, platoon commander. What followed was a lull, a truce of sorts, which lasted until the beginning of summer in 1995. As an experienced soldier by that time, I realised that the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina headed by their commanders made use of that time in order to prepare themselves for an all-out offensive in the area of the Nisici plateau. Indeed, it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was going on in that period, which, as you said, were preparation times? Were you able to gather any information on that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, for instance, that immediately before the offensive in 1995, in June, what became more frequent was artillery shelling on the part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As a soldier, it reminded me, or, rather, I could read from it that what would follow was an eventual offensive in the area of the Nisici plateau. We also received some information which pointed to the fact that the army of Herzegovina was preparing a large-scale and the strongest offensive as of yet against the Serb positions in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What followed in June? Can you tell us what things looked like in your area?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was early morning, between 4.00 and 5.00 a.m., although I don't know the exact date. In any case, I received a phone call from the Chief of Staff, Lieutenant Colonel Dusan Cacic, who informed me that we should be in the state of readiness since there was to be an attack against the positions of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did that look like? Were you able to find out which AB and H units were attacking you? As you said you had five tanks?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to notice anything as regards the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First we had one tank, then we had four. At that time, we knew that they had more tanks than we did. I don't know how many exactly though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What lines do you have in mind? Where was the separation line in your area and what did those separation lines there comprise?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area I'm referring to, which is the Nisici plateau, the lines of separation -- well, the distance between the belligerent parties was 800 metres at the minimum and in some places the maximum distance was 1300 metres. On average, the distance was some 1.000 or 1.200 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I just want the witness to clarify a bit where we are in time and where we are in space and where we are in terms of weaponry. I think the witness said before that when his brigade was established they had four tanks and now he said that at first they had one tank, so that is one question that I would like the witness to clarify. And, secondly, where exactly were those tanks deployed in June 1995? Could you please clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to conclude with that very topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that at first in the beginning you had one tank?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I also said that at the beginning, I was with the Ilijas Brigade and they had that one tank. What followed was that we received an additional four tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the exclusion zone was established you said that you received some tanks from Ilijas and other parts of Sarajevo who were in turn -- which were in turn brought to the exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you also said they were 30 kilometres away from Sarajevo at that point at the Nisici plateau?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Those tanks, were they ever moved from those positions, having in mind the things that followed? Did they ever return the same way they came from?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tanks that were -- that comprised the tank platoon when it was formed in 1994 were at the Nisici plateau. The tanks remained there until the end of war. The exact location was Jelik, the base there. They were not moved outside the immediate area of Nisici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Had it not been for the tanks and some other heavy weaponry which had been pulled out, what would have happened in the offensive?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, however, have I have to go back in time in order for me to tell you that before General Milosevic's arrival, we saw an expansion or the taking over of parts of territory held by the army of Republika Srpska. When he assumed command that trend was stopped. I'm saying this to try and show that General Milosevic did two great things for which I appreciate his work as a soldier. First and foremost, he stopped the offensives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the pull-out of heavy weaponry beyond the 20-kilometre zone. What was achieved in that way was that any possibility of taking over the road between the Nisici plateau, Ilijas and Vogosca was prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw that line on the map?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the separation line?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The direction of their operations by which they wanted to cut off the portions of that road.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is by way of information for the Judges. I wanted to show you another document, since you mentioned the offensive which began on the 15th. I wanted to ask you whether this document corresponds to what happened that morning and the following days. It is DD00-3323.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what does all this evidence indicate that is of benefit to your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not asking the witness about the casualties and the time, although he could tell us about that. He is explaining a military situation which was to determine the fate of both the troops and people in that area. He was at the Nisici plateau where the offensive began. Had it had been successful because it was carried out with the use of 150.000 troops, the road would have been cut off, the road between Vogosca and Nisici, all the way up to Vogosca, as well as the region in the north --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, how does it assist us in determining the issue of the liability of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to go back yet again to something I've already discussed here. I repeat that as General Milosevic's counsel, I believe that the intensity of activity of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time or, rather the position of the defence is that the activities of the SRK were by way of a response against the activities of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina rather than being directed at civilians. Also, the number of victims in the territory controlled by the SRK are a good indication of the intensity of activities conducted by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The intensity of fighting caused response on the part of the SRK, which was unavoidable. They were necessary to defend themselves rather than being a campaign directed at killing civilians and causing civilian casualties. The intensity of fighting had to reflect or, rather, impact the things that were taking place. It resulted based on the activity of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the number of victims is a good indication as to the intensity of combat. These actions were forced, rather, the SRK was forced to act. If we were to ask the witness how many casualties there were on the part of the SRK and Serbian civilians we would come up with a specific figure. However, what think is important for me to do is to show that the intensity of combat operations on the part of the ABiH was such that needs to be taken into account in the overall context. It had nothing to do with the campaign --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So your contention, then, is that the intensity of the fighting, negatives, contradicts the Prosecution's theory of a campaign of shelling and sniping. It contradicts the Prosecution's allegation of -- of terror, because you're saying that the terror inhered in the -- and was an outcome from the -- or of the intensity of the fighting. Let me just ask Ms. Edgerton just on that particular matter whether she has any submissions. This really is the -- is becoming now the -- clear to us to be the essence of the Defence case, that the intensity of the fighting necessarily prompted a response from the SRK and that intensity of the fighting contradicts any -- any allegation of a campaign and more particularly contradicts the allegation of terror because the terror was a natural outcome of that intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I -- just one or two sentences on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Even if the SRK responded because they were provoked, that doesn't allow them to respond indiscriminately at civilian targets. That's the Prosecution case. It's not responding to legitimate waging of war. It's responding indiscriminately by shelling civilian targets, by not engaging military targets, by sniping civilian targets as we have outlined in our schedules to the indictment. That is the Prosecution's case. So even if you respond to an action within an hour, perhaps with minutes, you have to respond to the source of fire and not to military targets. That's the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And not to civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we are understanding the case of both parties and that's the purpose of the questioning. Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic. Not on the topic. We have just concluded the discussion on that topic. Proceed with the questioning of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to continue in this spirit and to prove the intensity of the fighting in that location, I would like to show the witness two documents, DD00-3323. Can we zoom in a little bit on the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There was no translation when I initially received this a few days ago. Is there no translation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, is there any translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do actually have the document. Well, maybe I won't show him this document then. I will show him the other document. I'm sorry, I did -- I thought I had a translation but I don't have a translation. So perhaps instead of this document we can look at document DD00-28 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, if you wish to look at it, we can. It's very short. I mean, we do apply that practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wasn't objecting. I was just asking about the status of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want to bother you with that, but perhaps we can put a question about that document, so let us look at first then DD00-3323.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, then you will have to read it slowly and carefully so that the interpreters could translate it. You can read the heading. And can I please ask you to read the entire first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, command of the 4th Battalion of the 105th Mountain Brigade, strictly confidential number 105/4-1157 Ravanjsko Polje, 15th of June, 1995. Interim combat report. Section 1 to 25, Vares 2-4 and 4-4. Based on previously issued orders at 0600 hours on the 15th of June, 1995, offensive actions were launched in three given -- along three given axes." I think that it says "our main axis."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps we can place the document on the ELMO. It is better -- it's a better copy. It says "our tank."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Our tank and mortars fired about 10 tank and several mortar shells at enemy targets for purposes of preparation for an infantry breakthrough. The enemy responded or returned fire from Howitzers and mortars at our tank at Stuparovac and along the left wing in the section of the area of responsibility of the 2nd Company."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see that Stuparovo is mentioned here and you heard about this action and you already said something about combat over those few days. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proves what I said earlier, that Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina were actively preparing attacks at positions of the army of Republika Srpska, which is supported by this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please tender this document as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Ms. Edgerton is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because I wasn't objecting earlier doesn't mean I am not objecting now on different grounds. I see absolutely no connection in this document to anything to do with Nisici plateau which, in fact in and of itself, the witness has already testified is some 30 kilometres outside of Sarajevo, so my objection is then on two grounds, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Being what? Relevance and?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, relevance for two different reasons, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all of this is the area of responsibility of the SRK. This action along with this other document, this action at Stuparovo, so this action and the document that I will show indicates the axis of attack of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina precisely with the targets that they had in mind which the army of Republika Srpska had to protect and to which they responded in an adequate way. I believe that this document shows a specific situation whereby there had to be an appropriate military action in response to tank fire. On the day the offensive began, well, this document convincingly proves what happened on the 15th of June along all the lines of the front within the area of responsibility of the SRK. I already mentioned before a paragraph from the -- I'm going to repeat it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Given that it is 30 miles -- 30 kilometres from Sarajevo you would still maintain that it is relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if that line had been cut, 30 kilometres is a lot and it's not that much. The road within the area of responsibility of the SRK would have been cut. All the lines of the communication would have been severed and it would all have been finished in such a conflict which actually began then. Yes, it was 30 kilometres from Sarajevo but at that time it was all interconnected because at that point in time there was action along all the lines of the front, including from tanks which were the heaviest of weapons and this can be seen from this document. Last time I mentioned paragraph 53 of the adjudicated facts. I'm not going to repeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what's the significance of adjudicated fact paragraph -- well, 53, number 53. You call it paragraph, but I think it's number 53. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, number 53 of the adjudicated facts and that's one of the facts that we did not dispute. In 1993, about 75.000 soldiers of the 1st corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were deployed along the lines of separations around Sarajevo. Approximately a half were in the town itself, while the other half was at the lines of separations outside the town, precisely at the lines that he was talking about and where this fighting was conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But this adjudicated fact relates to 1993. Your document is relating to, if I'm not mistaken, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we showed that then there was 75.000 soldiers but in this action, through the document that we tendered, there were 150.000 soldiers in 1993, there was 75.000 soldiers along the lines of separation, but in this offensive that began on the 15th of June, there were over 150.000 because other corps also took part besides the 1st corps and we can see that from the documents that I'm going to show. So not 75.000 as it was in 1993, but in 1995 there were over 150.000 soldiers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. More thus. This was like this throughout the time of the war. There were lines outside and inside and it's a question who encircled whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So outside the city would embrace an area that is some 30 kilometres away from Sarajevo. Would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from the centre of Sarajevo. These would be the lines of separation. Ilijas was completely encircled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Nisici further up were also completely surrounded. These were the lines of separations, 220 kilometres, so this is the indisputed sentence in the adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My brother is asking, where is the number 150 that you just referred to? It doesn't appear in the document apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not here Your Honours. But we already tendered an exhibit earlier, orders from which it can be seen that the offensive began at all the lines of separation with the participation of other corps too. So that the total number can be seen from the documents that we already tendered through other witnesses. And also, there was something that was seen during the presentation of the Prosecution's case. From this document it can be seen that there was active direct fighting between tanks and other weapons at that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber by majority, Judge Harhoff dissenting, will admit the document. It's time for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, how much more time would you needing for examination-in-chief, because you're actually at the end of the time allotted to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Robinson, I have that in mind. I have one additional document, and I will close with it. Your Honours, the previous document was tendered but was not given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that document will be D281.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is DD00-2840. And we have a translation too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look at the heading, read out the date, and tell us what it is, who was ordered to do what; and the second paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, BH army 1st corps command. IKM, Igman. Military secret, strictly confidential. Strictly confidential number 01/1-222." Should I repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Igman, 15 June 1995, time 1400 hours. Report: To the command of the 12th, 14th, and 6th Division. All units. To the command of the 141st, 145th, and 146th Light Brigades."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The forces of the 3rd Corps with our 126th Light Brigade and the 134th Mountain Brigade/16th Division, liberated on their axis of attack the whole feature of Ravni Nabozic and Lipa as well as elevation 701, placing the Srednje-Semizovac road and the Semizovac intersection under their full control."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: We see that some of the units of the 1st Corps acted in unison with units of another corps, according to the second paragraph, that is?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened then? What was that road? We mentioned something about that in the previous document as well.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the road that I mentioned on several occasions. It goes through Semizovac, the Nisici plateau, Srednje onwards to Sarajevo and Vogosca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And as we can see here, it says they put the entire road under their full control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That day, the road was temporarily cut off. Our troops of the Republika Srpska as well as some of our sabotage units managed to regain the positions lost during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During that offensive of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which began on the 15th of June, how long did it last, approximately? Not only that action, but the entire offensive.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that intensive attacks lasted until the end of that month. I cannot recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: In the events in November 1994 but also during the combat in June, were there any casualties among the troops and civilians?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of victims, especially during the offensive in this area. There were many soldiers killed. I don't know the exact number, but with a degree of certainty I can tell you there were more than 25. As for civilian casualties, a bit earlier, before that, there was a mother and a daughter who had been killed by a Howitzer. It was on the 13th of June, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I would like to have the witness clarify which areas this document relate to, because I'm not completely familiar with the places and the names that are mentioned in the documents. The Ravni Naboznic and Lipa. So could you please ask the witness to clarify where these areas were that are mentioned in the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Harhoff, I will do so, since I seem to have forgotten. I wanted to ask that question too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show on the map where the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were? Perhaps you can take the pointer. You'll have to have your headphones on. Can you show where Srednje as well as the Semizovac intersection is.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semizovac, this is the Semizovac intersection, Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So they almost went as far as Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And they could have easily reached Vogosca cutting of any possibility of communication?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was exactly the arrow that I had drawn on the map. The axis of the main attack. It was a bottle neck by which they tried to interrupt the road between Semizovac, Ilijas and the Nisici plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was combat in settlements?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Through settlements trying to reach the road to Semizovac which would make it easier for them to take over other areas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Had the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina been able to reach Nisici, what would have happened with the Ilijas, Nisici, Hadzici --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At this point in time I would think my friend is asking the witness to do nothing more than speculate, especially given that the witness has said he was commander or deputy commander of the tank platoon in Nisici far to the north of that and hasn't said anything about where he was at the time in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, inquire from the witness where he was at that time. Let us see whether he has a basis for this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, how do you know this? Is this your personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And where were the -- rather, let me put my question in a different way. Were the other areas that are mentioned in the documents, such as, for instance, the Dobranjsko Brdo, were they also located in that area just north of Sarajevo that the witness has shown?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, it's another location of the 7th Corps. I didn't ask him about that. But he might have some indirect knowledge of that. These are the forces of the 7th corps and the 1st corps who were active at Jelasje and Dobranjsko Brdo. However in this location, it was the 3rd corps together with the 1st corps. The witness doesn't know much about the 7th Corps, which worked jointly with the 1st Corps at Dobranjsko Brdo. However, this is what he knows from his personal knowledge. On another location there was the 7th corps and the 1st corps and there were no 75.000 troops but, rather, twice as much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you are bringing this document to the witness, and I expect that you will also wish to see this document tendered into evidence. So if you want the Chamber to benefit from this document, then at least you should try and elicit from the witness which areas the document is really talking about or discussing. Now, I see two options and I just want the witness to say whether it's one or the other. Either the document deals with a number of locations which all of them are placed just in the vicinity north of Sarajevo; or the document deals with locations which are scattered all around Sarajevo. And that's my interest to find out, what does this document really address.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Harhoff, when I showed him this document, he said that he knew personally about the conflict in this area, where the 3rd corps were together with the 1st corps. I did ask him about whether he knows something -- well, first maybe can he go back to his seat and then I might ask him about any other knowledge that he possibly has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I mean, keep it simple. Let me ask the witness directly. Are you familiar with the other locations mentioned in the document, Mr. Witness? The Dobranjsko Brdo, the Zmijanice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I wanted to know. And please, Mr. Witness, you can sit down again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because I have one more question to you in relation to this document. And my question is about your comment a while ago that you felt that the -- that your brigade was encircled by the army of the Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct? Do you remember that you told us that it was your impression that the SRK or at least the brigade in which you were stationed felt that it was encircled by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Directly, when you look at the map and based on what I said, I couldn't have said that we were directly encircled but by cutting the road to which that refers to, we were -- well, the fighters were isolated as well as the civilian population and everything else. They would have been isolated had this happened. This is what I meant to say. But you can see that the Ilijas Brigade would have been completely cut off and would have been cut off from the free territory in the centre that was controlled by the army of Republika Srpska. And if we look at the map, then we can see that this is really so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I fully agree and I would interpret what we see in the same way. Now, my question is: What then do you make of the remark by General Karavelic in the first paragraph in which the general seems to suggest that he feels that the ABiH is encircled? I'm referring to the words in the first paragraph in which he says that the joint forces of the BH army achieved the following successes in the operation to break the siege of Sarajevo. That seems to suggest that at least General Karavelic was of opinion that it was the ABiH who was encircled by the SRK and that Sarajevo was under siege. Is that your impression? Do you share General Karavelic's observation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will just briefly say that I do not agree with that. When we look at the map, we see the breadth and the depth of the territory and everything around and what Mr. Karavelic said is not true. And that practically Ilijas is the only place that is practically in the encirclement and not the forces of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the city of Sarajevo, were they under siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier, when I was speaking and when I mentioned the municipalities that comprised the city of Sarajevo, I mentioned the municipality of Ilidza, Hadzici, and especially the municipality of Vogosca where I was -- well, my house in 1994 in the offensive but last came under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I fled to Vogosca. So if we looked -- I didn't mention the elevations above Vogosca, purely by accident. So it's not just Sarajevo. It's not that just the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was inside with Serbs around or the army of Republika Srpska. It wasn't like that, actually. If we take an elevation, for example if we go back to Zuc, that is a dominant elevation at -- in a specific territory where the lines of separation are about 100, 200 to 500 metres apart but the dominant elevation, I don't know its height, was held by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I state that with full responsibility, that it was really like that. My entire testimony is mostly focused on where I was, and that is the municipality of Vogosca, the Nisici plateau. But then we have Vogosca-Semizovac intersection, Srediste [phoen] and the Nisici plateau, that was the main communication for the population and the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have questions, but I would like to have this document, DD00-2840, tendered as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the translation that's in e-court in any case is incomplete and I wonder if it could be marked for identification until such time as it is completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What indicates its incompleteness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There appear to be two paragraphs missing from the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We don't have the next page in e-court, do we? I still don't see those two paragraphs and General Karavelic's signature. It may just be an e-court issue, then if Your Honours have a translation and a hard copy. Now we have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We admit it. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, just a question you know for clarification. I didn't want to interrupt you when you were dealing with the subject, but if you go to the transcript, page 17, line 18, 19, all the way to line 22, it seems that before General Milosevic took command, if I understood you right, and correct me if I'm wrong, the territory controlled by the army of Republika Srpska was increasing, and when General Milosevic took command he withdrew heavy weapons and, at the same time, he also stopped the offensives conducted by the ABiH. You are recognising him as a very good military man. But I don't really understand the logic behind this. He has got no weapons and he can still stop offensives. Whereas before him, there were heavy weapons and the territory was increasing. So could you tell us exactly how this could be possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that you misunderstood me. When General Dragomir Milosevic took the post, strong offensives of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were stopped, and up until he arrived the army of Republika Srpska was losing territories, before the arrival of General Milosevic. When General Milosevic came, he stopped those offensives, formed lines, and there was no further loss of territory, nor was any territory captured. The lost territories were not recaptured. We didn't understand each other. Perhaps you didn't follow me completely. There were no conquests, but the road was retaken. That was something that had to be done in order for the population and the soldiers to be able to continue to live. But the original positions, what was retaken were the original positions of the army of Republika Srpska, and I hope that this is now clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine. Thank you. So the fact that ABiH offensives stopped results from the military strategy and the military value of General Milosevic and not the use of special weapons, right? Because, according to you, heavy weapons had been withdrawn, so how did he manage to stop the offensive? Did you tell us how come the offensives suddenly started and the lines were now frozen? Were there special weapons or was it a very clever strategy? How did he manage to stabilize the positions? I mean you were a soldier and you can probably tell us what happened or maybe you understood what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lines were stabilized, well, first if you're losing a part of the territory, the line is shortened and simply then we would have more soldiers available, taking into account those wounded and killed and so on and so forth. That is one fact. The other fact is that new weapons came -- well, not new weapons but existing weapons such as Howitzers, mortars, tanks that I talked about, cannon, and that was deployed in the section where the attacks were expected, and I believe that there is nothing illogical there. I don't know anything about any particular or special types of weapons. I don't know what you're referring to there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My assistant tells me that the previous document that we tendered has not yet been given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document, document ID number DD00-2840 will be admitted as D282.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now, in relation to the question by His Honour Judge Mindua, you said that at the time when the heavy weapons were pulled out of the 20-kilometre exclusion zone the weapons, the tanks, the rest of the weaponry was transformed to the Nisici plateau outside of this area, far from this area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That weapon -- those weapons made it possible to set this up?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You were just giving evidence, Mr. Tapuskovic, when you said to the witness "Those weapons made it possible to set this up." You didn't allow the witness to proffer that evidence. But never mind. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djukic. You look as though you're feeling better.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions based on what you've said in testimony today, but very briefly, so you should be on your way home fairly soon, I would think, because you have had a long stay in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Judge Harhoff asked you a very specific question with respect to conditions within the city of Sarajevo and you answered him in detail. Just -- I'd just like to follow up on that and ask you: At any time during the war -- now let me rephrase that. You actually have no idea from your personal experience of what civilians inside the Bosnian-held territory of Metropolitan Sarajevo, the city centre lived through throughout the war, do you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Perhaps we didn't understand each other. What part of Sarajevo are you thinking of? I sincerely and honestly told you about those parts that I really know about. I told you about civilians in Vogosca, the population in the municipality of Vogosca. That's where my father lived as well as my mother. This is it what I'm talking about. As for the other municipalities that are part of Sarajevo, I think that they lived in a similar or identical way. Doesn't matter if they were in a different municipality or not. I think life there was similar as -- as the one in Vogosca, not similar, but identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if I said to you that from 1992 to 1995, civilians who lived inside Bosnian-held territory in the metropolitan area of Sarajevo were shot at frequently, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are your facts. I really don't know about things like that. I really cannot say anything about it other than that I never heard that any soldier or anyone shot at civilians. I really never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That wasn't quite my question actually. So let me go back to that. Would you agree with me that civilians within the metropolitan area of Bosnian-held Sarajevo were shot at over the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was shooting all over during the war. It was war. And you yourself said in the course of war, over the course of the war. And you probably have a different view of it than a soldier would. I mean, of course it was normal that there was one side and the other side of the conflict. We really cannot accept the fact that Serbs only -- it was only the Serbs who fired at Muslims or that Muslims only fired at Serbs. As I like to say, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired at Serbs and the army of Republika Srpska fired at Muslims. I mean, it was war. There was shooting. As to what extent and who happened to be aware, this is a very delicate and difficult question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And actually, with respect, Mr. Djukic, wasn't so difficult and I didn't ask anything about who fired at who. I simply asked whether you would agree that civilians in Bosnian-held territory, in Metropolitan Sarajevo were shot at frequently throughout the war. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you agree that civilians in Bosnian-held Metropolitan Sarajevo were frequently killed and injured by shelling and sniping, from 1992 to 1995? And remember, Mr. Djukic, I'm not asking who shot who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, are you asking him on the basis of personal knowledge or of information that he might have acquired?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can make it even more specific and ask on both grounds, Your Honour. That might clarify things for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, do you have any personal knowledge, and I mean -- by personal knowledge, I mean did you ever see with your own eyes or did you ever hear with your own ears about any civilians in Sarajevo, the metropolitan Bosnian-held territory of Sarajevo getting killed or injured by shelling or sniping from 1992 to 1995. So it is with your own eyes and your own ears.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly never saw or noticed anyone doing that, in view of the fact that my area of responsibility was further away. You're talking about the actual -- just one part of that town, and I didn't hear anything in particular about that, about sniper activities. I didn't hear really anything. But as for possible shelling, that some people were wounded by shells, that, I think, if there was shelling, and they happened to be somewhere, and then if they were -- I don't know. It's very hard, the way you put it. So it's not clear to me how because these were lines that were in close proximity. I don't know who could have fired what at whom. It's very, very strange.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you never saw or never heard anything but you gave a lot of evidence today about everything from hilltops to the placement of weapons and the location of confrontation lines which you yourself said was based on common knowledge, effectively. So perhaps I can ask you this: Did you ever hear in the media or from any other person or in any documents you might have received through your military command or from any off your colleagues or from any of your family who lived in areas around Sarajevo, that people who lived in Bosnian-held Sarajevo were regularly shelled and sniped at?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Did you ever see reports of it in the media, even in Crna?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the field where I was, we were frequently without electricity, but I watched reports from the media that things like that happened. But even that, to a limited extent. As for me seeing or noticing personally, I really did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you just said you watched reports from the media that things like that happened in answer to my question. So that sounds like you saw media reports to the effect that people who lived in metropolitan-encircled Sarajevo were shot and shelled. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for that you can take two answers. You can say that there was something like that on the part of the army of Republika Srpska, and to tell you truthfully if there were provocations from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the lines and places where the Serb population lived or that they were provocations via fire-arms, well, that's -- then I would say that as a soldier, there was a return fire once fire was received.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Djukic, I didn't ask you about provocations at all. Every single time I have asked you a question, I've asked you about civilians were in encircled Metropolitan Sarajevo. Did you hear of it, or see it, or learn of it, either through your own personal knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand a question being put once or twice, but to put the same question several times over, I don't think that that is proper. I'm sitting here and listening. I don't think that I ever repeated a question. I think at least that I did not repeat the one and the same question once. Now this is the third or fourth time that the same question is being put. He said that he didn't see anything with his own eyes and then -- then he moved to the media and then he gave two answers for that. And I think that it would be improper to continue in this vain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, I agree. The witness has already given an answer to the question. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, perhaps I can ask you one further question. The offensive of the summer of 1995 that you also spent a lot of time talking about in some measure of detail was actually effectively crushed by VRS and SRK forces, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, it was crushed by the army of Republika Srpska or by the army of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I don't know what you mean when you say pushed back or reduced. I didn't say that. I think the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, headed by General Milosevic, thwarted attacks, stopped them, and preserved the existing lines of the army of Republika Srpska, and I really tried to speak slowly and to be clear first to me and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, Counsel, as I understand is going further than that. She's saying that the offensive in the summer of 1995 that you testified about was crushed, crushed - it's a very strong word - I don't know how it is reflected in your language, but that offensive was crushed by the VRS and the SRK forces. Do you agree with that. It's not just a matter of General Milosevic thwarting attacks and stopping them but that the offensive was crushed by the VRS and the SRK forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I fail to understand. I've given an answer. For me, to crush something would mean that the side who managed to crush the enemy would advance further and deeper in the territory of the opposing side, which is not what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it was defeated without panic, with no problem. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether this was interpreted correctly, but it was said in B/C/S that there were defeated without any panic. It not clear in the least that they were defeated without panic. If interpreted in B/C/S properly, then, well, it makes it difficult to understand in my language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, witness? Counsel is putting to you that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the offensive was defeated and that there was not any panic accompanying that defeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm putting the question to you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you were able to observe, I smiled the first time I heard the question. We mentioned the fact that 150.000 soldiers attacked the area of responsibility of the SRK. We also mentioned the fact that the lines were almost broken around Ilijas municipality. And now we get this question which reminds me of a soccer game. I think I'm clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one point, Your Honour. The 150.000 number, and I've checked previously the transcript, from this witness's testimony never before came from the witness's mouth. It came from Mr. Tapuskovic's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic told us that testimony given earlier was to that effect. Did you say that, Mr. Tapuskovic? Because counsel is saying that this resulted from -- simply from what you said, not from testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is true. I said that it was based on a plethora of documents and evidence we've heard. I mentioned a figure when communicating with the Bench, when discussing the figure of 53 or rather the adjudicated fact number 53. Then I said that it stems from other documents as it does from this latest document that was tendered showing that the 3rd and the 1st Corps cooperated along the line where this person was. The witness did not say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I know the witness did not say that, but did any other witness prior to this witness say that, or was it simply a conclusion that you are drawing?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Robinson, I can show you the documents introduced through other witnesses although I don't have it here immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I would require you to do that; otherwise, this -- this would be -- I would consider this a very serious matter, if you suggested that evidence had been given and it turned out not to be the case but simply an assertion that you are making. So would you later today point to that evidence for me. And if you can, then Ms. Edgerton will owe you an apology. Ms. Edgerton, yes. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is very difficult for me to do that today, but I will do it as soon as I can. It is a number of documents that I have to assemble and present to you, but I will do it as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, because I -- I take it to be a person of integrity, Mr. Tapuskovic and that you would not mislead the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just so there's no misleading on the part of what I said, I was making that point with respect to the testimony before Your Honours today. Today. That had not -- those figures had not come from this witness's mouth. There had been no testimony that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well in that case, I agree with that. But Mr. Tapuskovic never sought to say that this witness had given testimony to the 150.000 number. I think what I understood him to be saying is that testimony given previously confirms that figure, not testimony from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. It was merely something that was adopted by the witness now and that's the point I was making, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, to finish up, and going back to your answers with regard to the June offensive, would it surprise you to learn that your general, General Milosevic, actually wrote to General Mladic and in that correspondence to General Mladic actually said this offensive that you've testified about in great detail today was stopped and crushed without any panic in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In those words, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And for the record, I can refer everyone to P738 in the English translation page 2, second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us hear the answer --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- of the witness first. Let us hear the witness's answer first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I understood it very well. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've talked about the seriousness of this offensive by the Bosnian forces, the size of the attack an its consequences on your side, in terms of both civilian and military effects. But what I'm putting to you now is actually your general reported to Ratko Mladic saying this two-month large-scale enemy offensive was stopped and crushed without any panic in 1995. Does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
