utterances.text: I am not particularly surprised. Perhaps I can explain. If an offensive is stopped or thwarted, if further advancement was prevented by the army of Republika Srpska in the Serb territory, and if vital roads are preserved, then it doesn't surprise me. I was a front-line soldier. As to what lingo they used in their office, that's a different thing. I hope you understand my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you would agree, then, with your general's report to the commander-in-chief, to the effect that the Bosnian offensive was stopped and crushed without panic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without panic ... yes. Unlike the previous offensives, when people left their homes and when there was destruction of property and when the entire population, the able-bodied ones and the other ones were trying to save their lives, judging the amount of panic among the soldiers and citizens, well, then, I guess that's what they had in mind, and I think it is justified when you see civilian population advancing or fleeing before the opposing parties' army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we did not understand the end of the witness's answer. Perhaps he could repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, would you just repeat the end of your answer, because the interpreter didn't quite understand it. Just the end of your answer, I think perhaps beginning "and I think it is justified," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that there no panic or that was alleviated because there was no population there that would flee the advancing army. That's what I had in mind. There were no movements of population. Instead, lines were formed, manned exclusively by soldiers in trenches and there in the territory. Therefore, we were prepared to face the offensive and we managed to thwart it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just a brief moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one last question perhaps to finish things off. So, Mr. Djukic, the way I understand your testimony now, having clarified matters, when you've said previously that you would not agree that Sarajevo was under siege, the basis of your knowledge is actually nothing, isn't it? Because you have no personal knowledge of civilians in the city centre being shelled or sniped and you heard nothing from the media. Your disagreement or your assertion that Sarajevo was not under siege is your opinion purely. It's your opinion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what time it is that you're asking me the same question, and I thought we were done with it. I think I gave a sufficiently clear answer. I lived with my family in a part of Sarajevo. We were refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think those are all the questions that I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one question only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djukic, you said when answering one of Prosecutor's questions that you did not see anything yourself concerning the plight of civilians in the part of Sarajevo that was under control of the ABiH. I'm asking you this: You said where you were at the time. Were you able to see anything concerning the plight of civilians in Sarajevo that was in the part of Sarajevo that was controlled by the army of Republika Srpska? Were you able to observe any of that in Grbavica, Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That doesn't arise from cross-examination, I submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, we don't agree with you. We think it does arise. Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I would kindly ask for the question to be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said you were unable to see and that you don't know anything about the things taking place in the part of the city that was under the control of the ABiH. What I'm asking you is this: One part of the city was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Do you have any knowledge of that? Did you see anything?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll turn over my chair to Mr. Sachdeva and take my leave, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The next witness is T-34, Milan Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. You may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you tell us your first and last name, or, rather, tell it to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: My name is Milan Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Even with the shortest of questions, please observe the screen in front of you. Only after the transcript has stopped, then answer. And the following questions can be answered by saying yes or no. You were born on the 11th of September, 1954?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Kalinovik in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You used to live in Sarajevo in Nedzarici in your family home from 1960?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your elementary and secondary education for a road transport technician in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your civic duty, that is the term with the JNA, was served in 1974, and you were a private?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the conflict broke out, you were employed with the PTT engineering in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges something about early 1992. Who did you work for then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: In March 1992, I was employed by UNPROFOR or the forces of the European union.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you begin working for UNPROFOR and what did you do exactly as early as 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a small clarification, because UNPROFOR and the forces of the European Union are different organisations, in my submission, so perhaps the witness can clarify which organisation he worked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Which one did you work for, the UNPROFOR or the European Union?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked for UNPROFOR. They wore blue helmets with the UN logo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do for them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I worked as -- as a car electrician.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were your tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Fixing the vehicles of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at that -- in that position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I worked with them until the 6th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain. When did you begin and when did you stop working for them, and why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Upon UNPROFOR's arrival to my company, I worked there as of day one until the 6th of May, when I was wounded returning home from work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, could you please ask the witness with which passport he was working within UNPROFOR? What was his nationality and was he wearing a uniform? I did not quite understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You need to explain this to the Judges, Witness. Explain where you were employed and how did it come about that you began to work for UNPROFOR? What was your work organisation and how did you end up working for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I worked in the PTT engineering from 1980 as an auto electrician. When the UNPROFOR came, they elected PTT engineering as the institution to be most suitable for their headquarters because we had satellite communications, telephone communications, and I signed a contract with UNPROFOR. I didn't need a passport, because I was born in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And since you put the question, I am of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I understood. I asked the question, because he said you worked for UNPROFOR and he also said that he had been wounded, so we could have thought that he was a military for UNPROFOR. Maybe he was a military electrician or something; hence, my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please then explain to the Judges how it came about that you were wounded? How did that happen? I don't want to suggest anything, but can you please explain how this happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: When I was returning from work, from PTT engineering, meaning I spent that day on my work duties at UNPROFOR, on my return from work, I was wounded in the Lukavica street, perhaps 200 metres from my house, from the direction of the Srakino Selo. I was walking like a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then and where were you then for an amount of time after that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I was taken to the hospital, actually first to the barracks. They gave me first aid and then they transferred me to the hospital where I was until the 27th of May, 1992, receiving medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you find out while you were at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I found out that my 65-year-old mother had been taken to a camp, that my father disappeared, that my wife and two children, aged 7 and 5, fled from there and that the house was set on fire, both my house and my father's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was your house till then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: It was in the Lukavicka 107 street at the base of Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have to take the break now. Before we break, I should make a clarification about the schedule for the rest of the week. Tomorrow's hearing will commence at 9.00 a.m.; Thursday's hearing will commence at 2.15; and Friday from 8.00 until 12.45. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just with respect to the last -- the last issue that my learned friend has broached with the witness, I am minded to object on the relevance of the evidence, but also it would be -- I suggest that counsel should establish the basis for the witness's knowledge, or, in other words how did he find out that these things took place. As it stands now, the witness was in hospital and the evidence is that he found out certain things. I realise I could ask him in cross-examination, but perhaps it's better to be done now, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you look at the matters that he found out, I mean, why would you be questioning the basis of that knowledge? Are you talking about the matters relating to his family?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm just asking just basically to establish how he found out while in hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, I don't see any need for that, quite frankly. Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I also think that he needs to tell you how he found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were at the hospital. How did you find out first about your mother and then about your father? Can you please tell us how you learned about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: At that time the PTT lines were still functioning and I found out from my family. I had a lot of relatives in Nedzarici. I found out that this happened to my parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to anyone on the phone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, explain that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of May, when I left the hospital, I called my uncle, the late Aleksa Tomanovic now, and I asked him if my parents were alive, if he knew anything about them, and he replied that people saw from the Skrkare house that my mother was taken away in the direction of Dobrinja V. They were not sure about my father, and then in a second conversation with him, I found out that my father was allowed to go to Lukavicka Cesta to cross the 10th transversal and to get to Lukavica but that he didn't get there and that he was most probably killed when he was about to enter the Lukavicka Cesta street or road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything about your father?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: No, not to this very day. I never found the remains of my father's body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell us if you ever returned to Nedzarici ever again after the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Once you learned that my wife had left our house, that my parents had the fate that they did and that the house was set on fire, there was no need for me to go back to Nedzarici. And the first time that I went back to Nedzarici was in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do, if you didn't return to Nedzarici on the 27th of May? Let's leave 2000 aside now. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: When I left the hospital, I joined the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before we continue, can you just please tell me if you ever worked in a hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have the rank of NCO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the Serbian Guard, and if you did, can you please tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I've heard of the elite Serbian Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever belong to the ranks of that guard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me whether any of your close relatives lived in Sarajevo throughout the conflict in an area that was under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a lot of family that remained in Sarajevo. They were loyal to the then authorities, including my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just briefly point out on the map of the city of Sarajevo several things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we do this quickly. This is document 2872.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the map to be shown, you were in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. In which brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I joined the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, the logistics battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: The brigade commander was Veljko Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: That was Mirosav Pandic, captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do in the rear or in the logistics section of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I repaired motor vehicles, the ones with wheels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the time that we're talking about, which part of town were you in now, as a member of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: That was Lukavica in the Slobodan Princip Seljo barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in on the map, in order to point out a few things. Can you please point out where the barracks was, where you worked?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I really have difficulty finding my way around a map. I never worked with a map, and Lukavica was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please scroll up a little bit. Can we scroll the map up a little bit, please. You can only see here -- you cannot see -- no, no. The other way. I would like to look at the southern part of the map. Scroll a bit more. A little bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now can you see?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness very well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: It's a little bit harder to find, but Lukavica is right underneath Mojmilo. I'm trying to find Mojmilo now. I think that is Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, well, let's not waste time. This barracks where you worked, how far was it from the line of separation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: 6 to 800 metres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the place where the barracks was, how far was that from Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the position of the place where the barracks was, in terms of the configuration of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Since I grew up on Mojmilo hill, that was the most dominant elevation, and the Slobodan Princip Seljo barracks was at the base of Mojmilo hill, in a plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell us, can you tell the Judges, where your brother's house or apartment was, in Sarajevo? Can you at least indicate that on the map, or can you say where that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you where it was. The apartment of my brother was in Dolac-Malta, in the very centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And throughout the war, that's where he lived?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: He remained loyal to the then authorities until he was arrested and taken to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please tell me, this place where you were with your family, was your family in Lukavica also?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the events that followed, were there any combat actions in which you yourself participated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And these combat actions, did it mean anything to you that your own brother was living in the centre of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, of course it meant something. It was important when we were provoked, at that point in time, unfortunately, I had to fire at my own brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During 1992 and 1993, did anything else happen to you personally in the course of combat?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 2nd of January, 1993, I was wounded at the technical workshop in the Slobodan Princip Seljo barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of a wound did you receive?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: It was extremely dangerous. It was a fracture of the skull and I had a very, very serious concussion and it was a life-threatening injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long were you on sick-leave?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I was on sick-leave until June 1993, late June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, you were wounded once, and then you were wounded the second time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever inflict a wound on yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: That's something that never occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell the Judges, if you can, when you joined the SRK, the barracks and the municipality of Lukavica, were there any heavy weapons there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: There were some at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you noticed and what can you confirm as having seen of the heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, I noted several tanks. There were two Pragas, and there were a few mortars a little bit farther away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you returned to your positions in mid-1993. Could you say if there was anything characteristic about 1994. Were you still at Lukavica, and are you able to say anything about what the situation was in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: In late 1993 and the very beginning of 1994 were marked by considerable combat actions and then onwards from May 1994, the -- lessened, I think some kind of a truce was signed. But I think that during the truces the highest casualties were among the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me if you found out anything about what happened with the heavy weaponry in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: After the truce was signed, our heavy weapons were pulled back from the town and they were placed under the monitoring of I will say the United Nations, again it was under 24-hour surveillance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know when Dragomir Milosevic took up the post of the SRK commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: The general came in August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the first months when he arrived, what were they like, the months from August on and then until the end of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: We were issued an order then. It wasn't a prohibition but an order that we were not permitted to fire from infantry or artillery weapons until mid-October, from what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And during the quiet period, was there any event that you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember a very striking image, an incident that happened a few steps away from me when two sisters, 14 and 16 years of age, went to the canteen to buy something because there was nowhere else where they could buy anything and they were hit or struck by a shell. One was killed and one was -- both of her legs were severed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in October 1994, or, rather let me ask you this first. Since you were in Lukavica, from that place could you observe anything at the foot of Hrasno?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: We couldn't see Hrasno, since it is beyond Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, my mistake. Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period, we followed civilians who moved together with soldiers entering the tunnel below the Butmir -- or underneath the Butmir airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any orders regarding that, since there was movement of troops there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Since our command was properly aware of the tactics of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina by which they mixed with civilians, our command expressly forebade opening any fire. They said we are not allowed to use even a slingshot, let alone a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in October, November and December in that area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. During those months, we were under attack along all of the lines of separation. It was a fierce attack, therefore I -- our command decided to take people who had work obligation to the front lines, since they were far more numerous than we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did things look like in Lukavica at that time, Lukavica and the environs, having in mind that there was fighting in other places as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: It was fierce. In Dobrinja IV, Dobrinja I, as far as I know, shells landed in settlements where civilians were in Lukavica, Toplik, Bijelo Polje and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After all those events in 1994, between October and December did something come about, something which is different?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Things got quieter after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Until May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What began taking place then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Then there was fighting again, infantry attacks, artillery attacks. They targeted military facilities as well as residential areas inhabited by civilians. There were many, many civilian casualties as well as among the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which period is particularly important? When did things escalate the most?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: This was all by way of preparation of theirs, I think. The assessment of our command was quite correct in that regard. They foresaw that things would get worse in -- in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are now in October but you were talking about May.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The worst situation was the last month and a half. There were fierce attacks on Trnovo, Vojnicko and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said something about a fierce attack and that they tried to stretch out your forces. Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: They attacked along the entire line of separation. Our scouts noticed the grouping of their soldiers above Trnovo. I don't know about the Ilidza theatre because I wasn't there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm just trying to establish the basis of the witness's knowledge. It certainly does not come across or did not come across in the 65 ter summary that Trnovo would be an area of discussion. Again, I could -- I could lead this in cross-examination, but the confrontation lines are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's just ask him, then. Witness, what is the basis of your knowledge? How did you acquire that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, which piece of information exactly are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The last answer that you gave, that they attacked along the entire line of separation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The attack that occurred was along the entire separation line. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, how did you know that? The question is, how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The separation lines were very close. In certain locations, only a road divided us. We would hear firing, that is, soldiers between each other talked and we would get information from our superiors, like platoon leaders or company commanders or battalion commanders and the rest. They would inform us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of those events, were you able to observe anything or did you participate in any combat operations at Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was attached to the Oslanska to the Cavarkapa [phoen] house were there was a particularly fierce attack in which we were outnumbered by far. And they had much better equipment too. However, we managed to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: To be specific, having in mind the question posed by my learned friend Mr. Sachdeva, I wanted to ask -- show you document D107. Witness, please read out the heading. We won't read the whole thing, but please read the heading and what follows immediately after, including the first paragraph, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Could I have a hard copy? Because after I was wounded for the second time, my sight worsened. I cannot see it too well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please read slowly. Read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: "Command of the 12th division. Strictly confidential number 02/2-7-10, Sarajevo, 26 June, 1995. Proposal of chosen targets to be destroyed and to tie up the aggressor forces by unit." Two -- should I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the order of the 1st corps, Chief of Staff, strictly confidential number 01/3-151, of 25 June, 1995, to carry out active combat operations in the zone of responsibility of all brigades, in the zone of responsibility of the 12th DKOV," I don't know what the abbreviation stands for, "in order to tie up the aggressor forces around the city and disperse them, offering relief to our forces outside the city in the zone of responsibility of the 14th and 16th DKOV."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you the following. We see a term here, which is tying up or dispersing or stretching out and you mentioned the very word before. Does that correspond to what you were able to see on the ground? Do you see any similarity between the document and the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please go to page 3 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can have it on the screen as well. At the bottom, 3 BB.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: "I approve the use of 3 RPG mines, 1 B/K for PA ASP, 1 B/K for AP, target 1 MG in Ponjarca street, first floor."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: "The group operator, RPG, also commander, assistant sniper, two automaticians."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, since I know where Danila Ponjarca street is. There was a fierce clash there for some five to six hours. We were trying to repel their attacks. We managed to do that in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties on your side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something more about the combat operations. We saw the date of the document. It was in June. Can you tell me what the things were like during that one month? How long did the offensive or those combat operations last?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Well, not only for one month. Maybe they were fierce for only a month, but there were clashes on a daily basis even after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the front line itself. I can tell Their Honours that my neighbour was killed by a shell which fell on a residential area. It probably overshot and he was killed in front of his own house. He was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether you know anything about an operation called Lukavac 93?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I have heard of that operation. It was aimed at Trnovo. I know about it. We were attached to Trnovo, or, rather to their defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you just repeat the last part of your sentence, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We, from the rear battalion, were attached for the purpose of that operation, the Lukavac operation, to them. We had very few fighters, and it was very difficult to defend Trnovo at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was an offensive operation on the part of the VRS; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Lukavac 93?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Oh, Lukavac 93, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about after the Lukavac 93 operation. Were there any other offensive operations by the VRS that you know of?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: No, there was no need to. I haven't heard of any other Lukavac operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is your function in the local community? Perhaps you can answer that question, but I should ask for the leave of the Bench, since I believe it is of some importance for the society in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Currently I head an NGO which deals with the families of the missing persons of the Sarajevo-Romanija region. I am the organisation's president.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of numbers do you have and I suppose you turn those over to the federation and the Republika Srpska pertaining to the number of missing persons in the area that used to be controlled by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was leading, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Reformulate the question, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This association of yours, were they able to establish anything about the fate of those who went missing during the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: In our organisation, we have the figure of 823 missing civilians of Serbian ethnicity during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me something else: During that part of your work, were you able to find out anything about your father? Do you have any information concerning him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that in 1998 the mortal remains of my father were taken to an unknown location. When that was happening, Ibrahim Sangic [phoen], an investigative judge was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect, my submission is that this evidence is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why do you say this is relevant, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about just the part that relates to his father, then maybe I could stop and then I would not have any more examination. I think my learned friend Mr. Sachdeva placed his objection at the point in time when I was asking about the witness's father, so perhaps I can then stop there and I have no further questions anymore. Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. So Mr. Sachdeva now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Mandic. My name is Manoj Sachdeva and I'm with the Prosecution and I'm going to ask you few questions today and possibly -- actually definitely also continue tomorrow. Can I just start by you recall that you gave evidence about two girls that were -- that had gone to the canteen and that were killed by shell. I think that's what you said. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that the canteen you speak about was the canteen at the Slobodan Princip barracks in Lukavica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you -- I understand that you were in the logistics battalion for the 1st Sarajevo mechanised brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you have a particular role in that battalion or were you just -- in other words, were you a commander of the battalion or were you simply working in that battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I was just a regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you were in the battalion from -- excluding the times when you were wounded, I take it you were in that battalion from 1992 through to 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: From the 27th of May, 1992 until 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in that battalion you told the Court that you worked with motor vehicles with wheels; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And presumably within the logistics battalion there were other persons or your colleagues worked on similar -- worked also with vehicles but did you also have colleagues that worked with ammunition or fuel? Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the logistics battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is it also right that the persons that a worked in the logistics battalion were not involved in combat or were not on the front lines? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: We went to the front lines if there was a need.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So when you gave testimony today that you were involved in combat, I think you spoke about the -- the difficulty of firing into Sarajevo because your brother lived there. I take it you were involved in combat as well as working in the logistics battalion. Am I correct in that understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And while you were in the logistics battalion, how often did you venture to the front lines and how often were you involved in combat? And if I may, I'm interested in the period in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: As I said, it was based on if it was necessary, if it was needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to the answer that you gave to counsel about the difficulty of firing into Sarajevo because your brother lived there, as a person working in the logistics section of the army, would you have been firing into Sarajevo? Would you personally have been firing into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never -- we never fired first. But if the lives of our children were concerned or my brother's life, then I would want to make sure they stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, that is not the question I was asking. You spoke about the difficulty of firing into Sarajevo because your brother lived there. And I want to find out whether, as a person working in the logistics section of the army, it would have been part of your duty to fire a rifle or some other weapon into Sarajevo. Was that part of your function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At certain points, yes. If we were attacked. Only in case we were attacked. But we would never fire at Sarajevo just like that. There was no reason. And let me also tell you that I only had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. Well, you had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And if it were necessary, you would have fired it. Would you have been called upon to fire it as a person working in the logistics section of the army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mandic, when you did venture to the front lines and when you were called upon to fire into Sarajevo, were you still part of the logistics battalion or were you part of another battalion; an infantry battalion, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: I was part of the logistics battalion at all times. But, as I said before, we were attached, because we didn't have that many men. We were attached to carry out combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was your brother, because you spoke about your brother who had remained in the centre of Sarajevo, was your brother a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: My brother remained loyal to the then authorities. He was taken to the front lines by force until he was arrested by some men who detained him and kept him until the end of the war, until the 18th of January, 1996. That's when he was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry to hear that, and my question, however, was slightly different. I just want to establish whether your brother was a civilian. I take it that he was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so when you told the Court that, if necessary, you had to fire into Sarajevo, and I think you told the Court that it didn't -- it didn't sit well with you because your brother was still living in the centre of Sarajevo. Is that how I understand your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it is right, is it not, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that we could also object to this question where there's insistence on firing at Sarajevo. He never said that he fired at Sarajevo. He said what were the circumstances in which he had to shoot. The question about firing at Sarajevo, I think is not appropriate, because he never said that he fired at Sarajevo. He said that sometimes in certain circumstances he was attached or he described the circumstances in which he fired. He explained that, but he never said that he fired at Sarajevo. That question is not appropriate. So that is the thrust of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to uphold it. I think the question is proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I just -- I'm going to repeat the question. When you told the Court that in certain circumstances you had to fire into Sarajevo, you also told the Court that it didn't sit well with you because your brother remained -- remained in the centre of Sarajevo? And is that -- is that a correct understanding of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He already answered that and said that is correct. You asked that already and he said that was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise, Mr. President. I didn't see the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mandic, it troubled you because often when fire was directed at Sarajevo, civilians would be killed and injured in the centre of Sarajevo. That's why it troubled you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: The activities, the combat activities that I spoke about were mostly clashes between front lines. And I never was deployed anywhere to be able to fire into the centre of Sarajevo. We mainly fought between Dobrinja IV, Dobrinja II and Dobrinja IV -- III.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So your brother did not live in the centre of Sarajevo. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDIC
utterances.text: No. My brother did live in the centre of Sarajevo, at Dolac-Malta.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that's why I'm asking you to -- well, I'm suggesting to you that the reason why you were troubled about firing into Sarajevo when -- when, as you said, when it was necessary, you were troubled because regularly civilians were hit, killed and injured by fire coming from the SRK?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has responded to the Prosecutor's question, not to my question, but to the Prosecutor's question in relation to this problem. He said that in the situation when I am faced with the choice of saving my children and firing at the other side, I would decide to fire on the other side and to protect my children. So I don't understand why there is so much insistence on this. The witness has already responded several times to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, no, he has not. This question is more specific. Witness, the question being put to you is that you were troubled because regularly civilians were hit, killed and injured by fire coming from the SRK. Counsel is suggesting that what is why you were troubled about firing into Sarajevo. How do you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said anything like that in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You never said what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that civilians were getting killed from fire opened by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not what counsel is saying. Counsel is saying that you were troubled, you were worried about firing into Sarajevo because civilians were regularly getting killed and injured by fire coming from the SRK. He's saying that that is the reason why you were worried and troubled about firing into Sarajevo. Is he right or is he not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is not right, and if you allow me, I will explain. I said that my own brother was taken to the front lines by force. That could possibly be Zuc, Dobrinja, Stup. It doesn't matter. And then when we had combat actions in relation to the enemy side, then I was thinking in my mind about perhaps if my brother had been brought there as a soldier, actually he never wore a uniform. He wore civilian clothing. A Serb there would be collateral damage. And that's when I said that that was when I had it in my mind that perhaps I could hit my own brother. But if the lives of my children and the life of my brother were in question, then I said that I would choose to protect the lives of my children. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On that note, we'll take the break and resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
